description.en: Learn tuples — immutable sequences perfect for fixed data — and how to unpack them elegantly.

story_variants.en:
## The Sealed Envelope

When you send a **sealed envelope**, the contents are fixed. You can read the letter inside, but you can't change it without opening a new envelope.

Python **tuples** are sealed envelopes — sequences you can read but never modify.

### List vs Tuple

| Feature | List `[]` | Tuple `()` |
|---------|-----------|------------|
| Mutable | Yes | No |
| Syntax | `[1, 2, 3]` | `(1, 2, 3)` |
| Use case | changing data | fixed records |
| As dict key | No | Yes |
| Speed | slower | faster |

### Tuple Unpacking
```python
coords = (10, 20)
x, y = coords   # x=10, y=20
```

> **Power move:** Return multiple values from a function using a tuple, then unpack at the call site.

### Named Tuples
Use `collections.namedtuple` when you want tuple speed but dict-like readability: `point.x` instead of `point[0]`.

### When to Use Tuples
- Coordinates, RGB colors, fixed pairs
- Function return values (multiple outputs)
- Dictionary keys that are compound
- When you want to signal data shouldn't change

props.code:
# Tuple creation
point = (3, 7)
rgb = (255, 128, 0)
single = (42,)   # note the comma!

# Access like a list
print(point[0])  # 3
print(rgb[-1])   # 0

# Unpacking
x, y = point
print(f'x={x}, y={y}')  # x=3, y=7

# Multiple return values
def min_max(nums):
    return min(nums), max(nums)

lo, hi = min_max([5, 1, 8, 3])
print(lo, hi)  # 1 8

# Tuples as dict keys
locations = {}
locations[(40.7, -74.0)] = 'New York'
print(locations[(40.7, -74.0)])

under_the_hood.summary: A tuple stores its item pointers inline in one fixed-size object that has no methods to change them, which makes it compact, hashable when its items are, and cheap to create.

steps.title: Fixed size, allocated once
steps.body: A list keeps its items in a separate array that can grow. A tuple puts the item pointers directly inside the tuple object, sized exactly at creation. There is no `append` because there is no spare room and no code that changes the slots after creation.

steps.title: Immutable container, possibly mutable contents
steps.body: The tuple's slots can never point somewhere else, but the objects they point to may be mutable. `t = ([1], 2)` followed by `t[0].append(5)` works and gives `([1, 5], 2)`. The tuple did not change; the list inside did.

steps.title: Hashable when its items are
steps.body: Because its slots cannot change, a tuple can compute a hash by combining the hashes of its items. That is why `(28.6, 77.2)` can be a dict key or a set element. A tuple that contains a list fails with `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.

steps.title: Packing and unpacking
steps.body: `lat, lon = point` compiles to UNPACK_SEQUENCE 2, which pushes the two items onto the stack and stores them into the two names. `a, b = b, a` packs the right side into a tuple-like pair and unpacks it, which is how the swap works without a temporary variable.

props.code:
point = 28.6, 77.2
lat, lon = point
a, b = b, a

stepDescriptions.description: Packing: the comma builds a tuple; no parentheses needed.
UNPACK_SEQUENCE 2: item 0 to lat, item 1 to lon.
Right side is evaluated first, then unpacked into a and b.

steps.title: Cheap to build
steps.body: The compiler turns a tuple of constants like `(1, 2, 3)` into a single constant stored in the code object, so it costs nothing at run time. CPython also keeps free lists of small tuples to recycle their memory.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Use a tuple when the shape of the data is fixed. You get a smaller object, a usable hash and free unpacking, and you document that the record should not change.
